questions.q: In the realistic project layout described, what does the `qsharp.json` manifest plus `src/*.qs` folder represent?
options: An optional folder that has no effect on compilation
The independently compilable, testable, and resource-estimable Q# project itself -- usable without any Python involved at all
A folder reserved exclusively for Python orchestration scripts
A deprecated structure no longer used by the modern QDK
questions.explain: qsharp.json plus src/*.qs forms the self-contained Q# project -- it can be compiled, tested, and resource-estimated on its own, with Python orchestration (experiments/) layered on top as a consumer.

questions.q: How does the Q#/Python project-structure boundary described in the lesson relate to Chapter 2's operations-vs-functions distinction?
options: There is no relationship between the two

Both enforce a clear separation between 'quantum algorithm, type-checked and resource-estimable' logic and 'classical orchestration' logic -- one at the language level (operation vs function), the other at the project-structure level (src/ vs experiments/)
Operations-vs-functions is about file naming conventions only
The project structure replaces the need for the operations-vs-functions distinction entirely
questions.explain: The lesson draws a direct parallel: just as the compiler enforces the operation/function boundary at the language level, separating Q# source into its own folder enforces the same kind of boundary at the project-organization level.

questions.q: How does Python code call an operation defined in a multi-file Q# project like `src/Algorithms.qs`?
options: By referencing the file path directly, e.g. 'Algorithms.qs.RunGroverSearch()'
By its fully-qualified namespace path (e.g. MyProject.Algorithms.RunGroverSearch()), not by which file it happens to live in
Python cannot call into multi-file Q# projects at all
Only the first operation defined in the project is ever callable
questions.explain: Operations are referenced by namespace path, which is independent of which specific .qs file under src/ they're defined in -- namespaces, not file names, are what Python code calls into.

questions.q: What happens automatically within an active qsharp.init() session when you edit a .qs file under src/?
options: Nothing -- you must manually run a separate rebuild command every time
Automatic recompilation is triggered when a Python cell re-runs and calls into the edited code -- no manual rebuild step is required
The entire Python session crashes and must be restarted
The edit is silently ignored until the next day
questions.explain: Recompilation happens automatically within the session when .qs files change and a subsequent call references them -- the gotcha is stale Python-side references to a previously compiled callable, not a need to manually rebuild.

questions.q: What is the actual gotcha the lesson warns about regarding recompilation, if behavior doesn't match a just-edited .qs file?
options: The .qs file syntax is always wrong in this case
A Python-side variable may still hold a reference to the old compiled version from before the edit, and re-fetching/re-calling is the first thing to check
Q# files can never be edited after the project is created
The qsharp.json manifest must be deleted and recreated after every edit
questions.explain: The lesson's gotcha is specifically about stale Python-side references to a previously compiled callable -- re-running the Python call to get a fresh reference is the first troubleshooting step, not assuming recompilation failed.
